claims.text: Conventional EAM references inadequately represent the wide range of atomic configurations sampled by ab initio high-entropy-alloy liquids near melting.
A deep neural-network potential can represent both solid and liquid configurations of a high-entropy material.
The proposed deep neural-network potential will capture the diverse configurations of ab initio high-entropy-alloy liquids near their melting points.
The reference potential should be trained by active learning on ab initio solid and liquid configurations.
Using a deep-learning reference will improve reference–target phase-space overlap relative to an EAM reference.
High-entropy alloys are systems containing at least five principal elements.
The intervention is applicable at temperatures at or above approximately 0.9 Tm.
The intervention should be especially effective for refractory high-entropy alloys whose melting temperatures are typically above 2000 K.
Near-melting liquids contain short-range order and diverse local atomic environments that a deep-learning potential can capture more accurately.
Active learning ensures that the training set is broad and representative of configurations in both solid and liquid phases.
A representative solid-and-liquid training set causes the learned reference distribution to overlap more closely with the ab initio phase space.
Improved phase-space overlap reduces interpolation errors and thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to an EAM reference.
The deep-learning reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD with conventional EAM references.
The deep-learning reference will yield free energies closer to independent ab initio benchmarks than the EAM reference.
The method may be less effective when phase separation or ordering occurs outside the training regime.
The effect size depends on the quality and configurational diversity of the deep-learning training set.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing EAM- and deep-learning-referenced thermodynamic integration for the same alloy near melting against an independent ab initio free-energy benchmark.
Failure to obtain both a statistically significant mismatch reduction of roughly 30–50% or more and closer agreement with the independent ab initio benchmark would falsify the hypothesis.
